beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Adwait Changan, and this video is about what a second AI agent actually costs you. Today we are going to learn why adding agents makes a system less reliable, not more, and what the number has to be before a team of them beats one. The arithmetic is unkind and almost nobody does it.

show.event: composer on cream; the fellow names himself and the topic

props.command: If one agent works, do five work five times better?
output: Adding agents buys parallelism and costs coherence.
If every step must succeed, reliability compounds downward, fast.
Most multi-agent wins are one agent with better tools.

beats.narration_text: A second agent gives you exactly two things. Parallelism, because two things can happen at once. And specialisation, because each one can carry a narrower set of tools and a shorter brief. Those are real. Everything else people claim for multi-agent systems is downstream of those two.

layers.title: Parallelism
layers.sub: two things can happen at the same time

layers.title: Specialisation
layers.sub: narrower tools, shorter brief, less to confuse

layers.title: And a bill
layers.sub: coordination, and reliability that compounds downward

props.caption: The first two are real. The third is the one nobody prices.

beats.narration_text: Start with the cheap cost, coordination. A supervisor talking down to workers and back grows gently: eight agents, fourteen links. But if you let them all talk to each other, eight agents is twenty-eight connections. Same eight agents, twice the surface area, and every link is somewhere a handoff can be misread.

show.event: the header and small counts write on
eight agents lands: 14 against 28, in terracotta

beats.narration_text: Put ninety-five percent into it, which most people would call a good agent. One agent fails five runs in a hundred. Three agents fail fourteen. Eight agents fail thirty-four. You did not make anything worse at any step. Every one of them is still ninety-five percent.

show.event: eight agents lands at 66.3%, in terracotta

props.artifactHeading: Nothing got worse. The chain did.
artifactLines: agents   end to end   failures/100 runs

beats.narration_text: The honest caveat is that this arithmetic assumes every step must succeed. Some systems are not like that. If agents vote, or retry each other, or you only need one of five to find the answer, the maths inverts and more of them genuinely helps. The question is which shape you actually have.

props.title: Unless They Do Not Chain
props.body: If agents vote, retry each other, or only one of five needs to succeed, the arithmetic inverts and more genuinely helps. Know which shape you have.

beats.narration_text: So, the verdict. A second agent buys parallelism and specialisation, and charges you coordination and compounding reliability. Coordination is the forgiving half: eight agents under a supervisor is fourteen links, though letting them all talk is twenty-eight. Reliability is the expensive half. At ninety-five percent each, with every step required, eight agents fail thirty-four runs in a hundred while no individual agent got any worse. Turned around, eight agents must each hit ninety-nine point four percent just to match what one agent at ninety-five already does. Add agents when the work genuinely parallelises and a wrong handoff is cheap to catch. Otherwise you want one agent with better tools.

props.artifactHeading: More agents is a bill, not an upgrade
artifactLines: A second agent buys parallelism and specialisation. It charges coordination and reliability.
Supervisor topology is forgiving: 8 agents, 14 links. A mesh is 28.
At 95% each with every step required, 8 agents fail 34 runs in 100 — nothing got individually worse.
To reach 95% end to end, 8 agents must each hit 99.36%. That is the bar to merely match one.
Unless the work parallelises or they vote, you want one agent with better tools.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt. Here is a multi-agent design I am considering. Tell me which steps genuinely run in parallel and which must happen in order. For the sequential ones, compute the end-to-end success rate if each agent is ninety-five percent. Then tell me what one agent with all the tools would have to get wrong for the split to be worth it. Run it before you build. That last question is usually the whole answer.

props.command: Here is a multi-agent design I am considering. Which steps genuinely run in parallel, and which must happen in order? For the sequential ones, compute end-to-end success if each agent is 95%. Then: what would one agent with all the tools have to get wrong for the split to be worth it?
output: Most designs have far fewer genuinely parallel steps than they look like they do.
If you cannot say what one agent would get wrong, you do not need two.

beats.narration_text: That is the short version. The full video shows the end to end arithmetic in code, and the case where it inverts. Watch Multi-Agent Systems for the whole argument. The link is right below.
